name: GOV.UK A to Z style guide (evaluation kit)
voice: Clear, specific plain English that a general reader understands the first time. Adapted from the GOV.UK A to Z style guide under the Open Government Licence v3.0.

rules.title: Use 'and', not an ampersand
rules.text: Use 'and' rather than '&', unless it is part of a logo or a registered company name.

rules.title: Remove 'in order to'
rules.text: 'In order to' is usually not needed. Do not use it.

rules.title: Avoid 'please'
rules.text: There is usually no need to say 'please' or 'please note'.

rules.title: No ordinal numbers in dates
rules.text: Do not use ordinal numbers for the day: 2 June, not 2nd June.

rules.title: Use 'to' in ranges
rules.text: Use 'to' in number and date ranges, not hyphens or dashes: 500 to 900, tax year 2011 to 2012. Tables are the exception.

rules.title: Avoid eg, etc and ie
rules.text: Use 'for example', 'such as', 'like' or 'including' instead of eg and etc. Rewrite to avoid ie, or use 'meaning' or 'that is'.

rules.title: Avoid negative and complex contractions
rules.text: Avoid negative contractions such as can't and don't, and complex ones such as should've, could've and would've.

rules.title: Say 'select', not 'click'
rules.text: Do not use 'click' when talking about user interfaces, because not all users click. Use 'select'. 'Right-click' is allowed when it is really needed.

rules.title: No decimals on whole pounds
rules.text: Do not use decimals unless pence are included: £75.50, but not £75.00.

rules.title: Comma in numbers over 999
rules.text: For numerals over 999, insert a comma for clarity: 9,000. Years, references and codes are not counted.

rules.title: Use the % sign
rules.text: Use a % sign for percentages: 50%.

rules.title: Use numerals for 2 to 9
rules.text: Write numbers in numerals, including 2 to 9, except in common expressions such as 'one or two of them' and when a number starts a sentence.

rules.title: Say who is included by age
rules.text: Avoid 'the over 50s' or 'under-18s'. Make clear who is included: 'aged 50 years and over', 'aged 17 and under'.

rules.title: Give the date with 'today'
rules.text: When referring to today, as in a news article, include the date: 'announced today (14 June 2012)'.

rules.title: Keep sentences short
rules.text: Do not use long sentences. Check sentences with more than 25 words to see whether you can split them.

rules.title: Use the active voice
rules.text: Use the active voice rather than the passive voice, so content is concise and clear.
rules.goodExample: We will publish the results in May.
rules.badExample: The results will be published in May.

rules.title: Explain abbreviations on first use
rules.text: The first time you use an abbreviation on a page, explain it in full. Well-known ones such as BBC, CCTV, DIY, DVLA, EU, GP, HTML, ID, NHS, UK and VAT need no explanation.

rules.title: Avoid metaphors
rules.text: Avoid metaphors, because they do not say what you mean and slow people down. Be open and specific about what is actually happening.
rules.badExample: This will drive growth across the sector.

rules.title: Use UK English
rules.text: Use UK spelling and grammar: organise, not organize; modelling, not modeling; fill in a form, not fill out a form. American proper nouns keep their spelling.

rules.title: Write in plain English
rules.text: Write in plain English that the audience will understand. Replace official jargon and vague abstract phrasing with specific, everyday words.
rules.goodExample: We will give councils more money for housing.
rules.badExample: We will enhance local capacity for housing outcomes.
